symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots on leaves, often with yellowing around affected tissue.
Raised scabby spots may appear on fruit and stems.
Leaf spotting can merge under warm, wet conditions and cause leaf drop.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather with frequent rain, overhead irrigation, or long leaf wetness.
Dense canopy and poor air movement.
Contaminated seed, seedlings, tools, or crop residue.
prevention: Use healthy seedlings and avoid moving through the crop when leaves are wet.
Improve spacing, staking, and pruning to reduce leaf wetness.
Remove infected crop residue after harvest and rotate away from tomato and related crops where possible.
ipm_measures: Rogue badly affected plants early if infection is localized.
Prefer drip irrigation over overhead watering.
Use copper or other locally recommended bactericide only under agriculture expert guidance and label directions.
safe_input_guidance: Do not mix chemicals casually or repeat sprays without field confirmation.
Follow the product label, waiting period, protective equipment guidance, and local extension recommendations.
Avoid unnecessary pesticide use when the diagnosis confidence or field symptoms are unclear.
when_to_contact_expert: Rapid spread after rain or irrigation.
Spots on fruit or widespread leaf drop.
Unclear symptoms, low model confidence, or repeated failures after basic sanitation.

symptoms: Brown leaf spots with target-like concentric rings, usually beginning on older lower leaves.
Yellowing around spots followed by drying or leaf drop.
Stem lesions or fruit shoulder lesions may appear in severe cases.
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid weather and repeated leaf wetness.
Nutrient stress, weak plants, or older foliage.
Infected crop debris and volunteer tomato plants.
prevention: Stake plants and remove lower infected leaves carefully.
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves.
Maintain balanced nutrition and avoid plant stress.
ipm_measures: Remove infected leaves and destroy crop debris away from the field.
Improve airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.
Use locally recommended fungicide only after extension-worker validation and label-based application advice.
safe_input_guidance: Do not apply broad-spectrum fungicide only because a phone image looks suspicious.
Use the least-risk option recommended locally and respect harvest interval instructions.
Keep spray records for follow-up monitoring.
when_to_contact_expert: Many lower leaves show ringed spots.
Disease appears during flowering or fruiting.
The app risk level is HIGH or neighboring confirmed cases are reported.

symptoms: Large water-soaked patches on leaves that quickly turn brown or black.
White fuzzy growth may appear on leaf undersides during humid mornings.
Fruit may develop firm greasy brown lesions.
favorable_conditions: Cool to mild temperatures with very high humidity, fog, rain, or long leaf wetness.
Cloudy weather and dense crop canopy.
Nearby infected tomato or potato crops.
prevention: Scout frequently during wet weather and remove suspicious plants early.
Keep foliage dry when possible and improve field ventilation.
Avoid planting near infected potato or tomato residue.
ipm_measures: Treat suspected late blight as urgent because spread can be fast.
Isolate or remove heavily infected plants after expert advice.
Use protective fungicide programs only as recommended by local agriculture officers and label directions.
safe_input_guidance: Do not delay expert contact if symptoms match late blight during wet weather.
Do not overdose or shorten spray intervals beyond label instructions.
Use protective clothing and observe pre-harvest intervals.
when_to_contact_expert: White growth appears under leaves in humid conditions.
Fruit lesions are present or the risk checklist flags humidity and rainfall.

symptoms: Upward curling of young leaves with yellowing and reduced leaf size.
Flower drop and poor fruit set, especially if infection starts early.
favorable_conditions: Warm dry periods that favor whitefly multiplication.
Nearby infected tomato plants or susceptible weeds.
prevention: Use healthy seedlings and inspect nursery plants before transplanting.
Remove infected plants early to reduce virus source.
Manage weeds and volunteer tomato plants around the field.
ipm_measures: Use yellow sticky traps and record whitefly counts.
Use insect-proof nursery protection where possible.
Prefer integrated whitefly management with expert guidance; chemical control alone cannot cure infected plants.
safe_input_guidance: Do not expect pesticide spray to cure virus-infected plants.
Avoid repeated insecticide use without monitoring whitefly counts.
Rotate control methods only with local expert guidance to reduce resistance risk.
when_to_contact_expert: Young plants show curling, yellowing, and stunting.
Whitefly counts are rising in traps.
Several nearby farms report similar symptoms.

symptoms: Leaf appears broadly normal with no strong visible disease pattern detected.
Minor marks may be caused by age, dust, nutrition, water stress, or image quality.
favorable_conditions: Continue monitoring because disease risk can still rise with weather and nearby outbreaks.
Flowering and fruiting stages need closer scouting even when the current leaf looks healthy.
prevention: Keep regular field scouting twice a week and after rain.
Maintain balanced irrigation, nutrition, sanitation, and weed control.
Use pest traps to catch early whitefly or moth pressure.
ipm_measures: No disease treatment is recommended from this image alone.
Recheck if symptoms appear on multiple plants or spread across the field.
Log trap counts and weather conditions for follow-up monitoring.
safe_input_guidance: Avoid preventive pesticide use without a clear pest or disease reason.
Save input cost by monitoring first and acting only when evidence supports action.
when_to_contact_expert: Symptoms appear later or spread quickly.
The model confidence is low or the photo quality is poor.
Neighboring confirmed cases are reported nearby.
